name: Karl Nakamura

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for any company, union, party or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so feel free to tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work for Arnold Pike up at High Rigg, which is a hill farm, four hundred ewes on the fell and a few low fields for hay and a bit of oats. Arnold's seventy-one and his son went to the city, so it's mostly me and him and two dogs, Moss and Jess. Most days I'm up on the quad bike checking the flock, mending walls, moving sheep down when the weather turns. Gathering in autumn is the best day of the year, every farm in the valley helps each other.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like being out on the hill on my own with the dogs, honestly, nobody bothers you. What wears me out is the money, the pay's poor and the sheep barely pay for themselves. My wife Anna does a few hours in the school kitchen and we rent a cottage in the village, and we've got a couple of weeks put by. I don't hold with the AI things, I've never used one and I've no wish to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hype. Aye, I'd have guessed as much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say told you so, and I'd say it at chapel and at the auction mart. Plenty of the old boys would agree with me. I don't go online much, Anna does that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means things carry on, which suits me. Sheep on a fell don't care about computers. The hardest thing on this farm is a ewe stuck in a snowdrift, and no computer is digging her out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on, same as always. Keep the walls up, get through lambing, try to put a bit aside after the lamb sales. Not touch any of the apps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Same as most years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What worries you most in a normal year, then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Whether Arnold keeps going. He's seventy-one and his knees are bad. If he sells, the land probably goes to a big estate or gets planted with trees, and then there's no job for me up there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you think should help farms like High Rigg stay going?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not the government, I don't want handouts. I'd want a fair price for lamb from the supermarkets, and young people taught the trade by the old ones, like Arnold taught me. That's how it's always worked.

S0.say: Told you so, he'd say at chapel and at the auction mart, where the old farmers would agree. He doesn't go online much.
S0.think: Things carry on, which suits him. Hill sheep don't care about computers and the hardest jobs still need a person.
S0.do: Carries on mending walls and getting through lambing, and puts a little aside after the autumn lamb sales. Avoids AI apps entirely.
S0.quote: The hardest thing on this farm is a ewe stuck in a snowdrift, and no computer is digging her out.
S0.fieldNote: Karl's real worry is his 71-year-old boss retiring and the land being sold or planted with trees. He rejects government help and wants fair prices and apprenticeships instead. His sense of the hill as beyond technology's reach is strong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Many jobs. Well, not on a fell, I'd think.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say every generation has its new gadget and the hills are still farmed by men and dogs. At the mart I'd say the lowland farms can have their robots. I'd be a bit dismissive, if I'm honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I don't think it touches me much. Arnold's not going to buy a robot at seventy-one, he won't even use the phone for the bank. A robot that can gather four hundred ewes off a fell in fog would have to be better than Moss, and she's the best dog in the valley.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going, nothing different. If the lowland farms started using robots, I'd keep an eye on whether they took the contract work I do in winter, hedging and fencing. Otherwise I'd wait and see.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. A little bit of worry about the winter work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much of your income is that winter contract work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe a fifth. I do hedging and fencing for two lowland farms in January and February. If a machine did that, it'd hurt, but I'd still have High Rigg.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the hills are farmed by men and dogs. Are there women farming up there too?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There are, Arnold's late wife ran the sheep half the time. I just meant people, not machines. Anna would tell me off for that one.

S1.say: Every generation has its new gadget, and the hills are still farmed by people and dogs. The lowland farms can have their robots.
S1.think: It wouldn't touch him much because his elderly boss won't buy a robot. A machine would have to beat his best dog at gathering in fog.
S1.do: Carries on as normal. Watches whether lowland farms automate the hedging and fencing contract work he does in winter, about a fifth of his income. Otherwise waits to see.
S1.feel: Mostly calm, with slight worry about his winter work.
S1.quote: A robot that can gather four hundred ewes off a fell in fog would have to be better than Moss, and she's the best dog in the valley.
S1.fieldNote: Karl trusts the fell and his dog more than any machine, and his boss's age reinforces that. The one crack is the winter contract work on lowland farms. He corrected himself about women farmers when asked, gently.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. With robots that can do hands-on work. That's not right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's wrong, and people who run these companies don't know what they're doing to places like ours. I'd say it at chapel and I'd say it to the MP if he came round. I'd want the government to stop the big companies from just rolling over everyone, which isn't what I'd usually say.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think it'd be the end of High Rigg. Arnold would sell, and whoever bought it would run it with robots and drones from a laptop somewhere. I don't know any other work, and I won't take charity. I'd be twenty-nine, and the only thing I'm good at would be something a machine does better.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop all spending we didn't need, straight away, no more pub on Fridays. I'd ask around the chapel and the valley for any work going. If it came to it, we'd move in with Anna's parents, they've got a farmhouse with room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd be lying awake.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you won't take charity. If there were government payments for people who lost their jobs, would you take them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want not to. Anna would make me, probably. I'd take it and feel bad about it, and I'd pay it back somehow if I could.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Arnold?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say don't sell to them. He'd say he has to, he's got nothing else for his old age. And he'd be right, and I'd shake his hand.

S2.say: It's wrong, and the people running these companies don't understand what they're doing to places like his. He'd want the government to rein in the big companies, which isn't his usual view.
S2.think: It would end the farm he works on, sold and run by robots from afar. He knows no other work and doesn't want charity.
S2.do: Cuts all non-essential spending, including Friday nights at the pub. Asks around the chapel and valley for work. Moves in with his wife's parents if needed.
S2.quote: I'd be twenty-nine, and the only thing I'm good at would be something a machine does better.
S2.fieldNote: This pushes Karl to want government action against companies, against his usual free-market view, and he notices it himself. His resistance to handouts softens only because his wife would insist. He wouldn't blame his elderly boss for selling.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. Arnold would be seventy-six. He'd likely have sold anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we should be putting our young people into trades that'll last, and the chapel and the valley should look after their own. I'd say it plain, I don't dress things up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think five years would make little difference to me, because I wouldn't do much with it. I'm not going to go and learn robots. I'd spend five years telling myself the fell is different, and then find out it isn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd try to save more, maybe forty a month, and sell the old quad bike I don't really need. I'd keep working for Arnold and doing the winter contracts. I'd probably not do much else, if I'm honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. Maybe more, because I'd see it coming and still not move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: That's an honest thing to say. Why wouldn't you move?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I don't know what I'd move to. Everything I know is up there, the walls, the dogs, the weather. You can't learn a new life in five years at my wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do the extra three years buy you, compared with the two-year picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit of money in the bank, maybe. And a bit longer with Arnold on the hill. It doesn't change how it ends.

S3.say: Young people should go into trades that will last, and the chapel and valley should look after their own. He'd say it plainly.
S3.think: Five years would make little difference because he wouldn't act. He'd keep telling himself the fell is different until it wasn't.
S3.do: Saves about forty a month and sells an old quad bike he doesn't need. Keeps working on the hill farm and doing winter contracts, with little else changed.
S3.feel: Alarmed, perhaps more so because he'd see it coming and still not move.
S3.quote: I'd spend five years telling myself the fell is different, and then find out it isn't.
S3.fieldNote: Karl is unusually frank about his own inaction, saying he'd see it coming and still not change. He doesn't see how to learn a new life on his wage. The extra time to him means savings and time with his boss, not a new path.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. Arnold would be gone by then, most likely. God rest him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the hill farms will need people even if the lowlands don't, and we should fight for that. I'd talk to the farmers' union about keeping hill farming going, for the landscape and the community. That's about as political as I get.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think ten years gives me a chance at something, maybe taking on a tenancy on a small hill farm if one came up, and being my own boss. Or the estate that buys High Rigg might want someone who knows the fell to keep an eye on the robots. I'd sooner be the shepherd of the robots than not up there at all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd save what I could, forty a month, maybe more if Anna got more hours. I'd keep working for Arnold and watch for any tenancy coming up. I'd wait a few years before deciding anything, because ten years is a long time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Less than before, but it's still there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you learn the robots, if it meant staying on the hill?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If that was the only way to stay up there, I suppose I would. Arnold would laugh at me. I'd learn it the way I learned the dogs, slowly and with a lot of swearing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does it change anything for you and Anna, family-wise?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd still want children. Chapel matters to us, family matters. We'd just want to know there was work before we had them, so maybe we'd wait a bit.

S4.say: Hill farms will need people even if the lowlands don't, and that's worth fighting for. He'd talk to the farmers' union about keeping hill farming going for the landscape and community.
S4.think: Ten years might let him take a small hill tenancy or stay on as the person watching the robots for a new owner. He'd rather do that than leave the hill.
S4.do: Saves about forty a month. Keeps working for his boss and watches for a small hill tenancy to come up. Waits a few years before making any bigger decision.
S4.feel: Anxious, though less than in the faster pictures.
S4.quote: I'd learn it the way I learned the dogs, slowly and with a lot of swearing.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade, Karl will grudgingly consider learning the robots if it keeps him on the hill. His dream is a small tenancy of his own. He and his wife would delay children rather than give up on them.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. High Rigg sold, no work, and me with nothing else I know. What would help is not handouts, but tenancies for young farmers on the hill, and the old ones paid to teach us, like apprenticeships.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask about the land. Everyone talks about jobs, but it's the land too. If robots farm it from a laptop, nobody's there to keep the walls up or notice the beck's flooding. That's a loss you can't count.

headlineQuote: I'd sooner be the shepherd of the robots than not up there at all.
portrait: Karl Nakamura is a 27-year-old who works a 400-ewe hill farm for an elderly farmer, out on the fell with his two dogs. He rents a village cottage with his wife Anna, who works in a school kitchen, with a couple of weeks saved. Traditional and chapel-going, he wants fair prices and apprenticeships, not handouts, and has never used AI. He stays calm in a plateau and in steady change, sure the fell is beyond robots. AGI in two or five years alarms him, and he admits he'd see it coming and still not move. With ten years he'd grudgingly learn the robots to stay on the hill or take a small tenancy.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most: the hill farm sold, no work, and nothing else he knows how to do.
whatWouldHelp: Hill tenancies for young farmers and paid apprenticeships where older farmers teach the young, rather than handouts.
